findings.detail: "be keep something shut" is not English — the importer copied a malformed Wiktionary line (candidate_glosses index 0 reads "to be keep something shut") verbatim, so the defect survived the shortening step. The verb means to hold something shut: die Tür zuhalten, sich die Nase zuhalten, sich die Ohren zuhalten.

"turn something" drops the directional zu- that is the entire content of the verb, and kaikki's index 0 ("to turn (rotate) something") actively pushes toward the wrong reading: zukehren is not rotating, it is turning a side of something toward a person or place. Its dominant use is jemandem den Rücken / das Gesicht zukehren.

The shortening dropped the parenthetical that carried the meaning: kaikki index 0 is "to feed (a liquid, electricity, etc.)", and bare "feed" reads as füttern, a verb zuleiten never means. Zuleiten is to channel or supply something along a conduit — Wasser, Strom, Frischluft zuleiten — and by extension to forward a document to an office.

"suture" is a surgical term, but zunähen is the ordinary domestic word for sewing something closed — ein Loch, eine Naht, eine Tasche zunähen. The register mismatch will keep a learner from using the verb where it actually belongs. candidate_glosses index 1 ("to stitch up") is the everyday equivalent.

"hurt" is a weak Wiktionary gloss the importer took at face value. Zurichten is not the German for hurting someone — that is verletzen or wehtun — and in current usage it appears almost exclusively as übel/schlimm zurichten, meaning to batter someone or leave something in a wrecked state. Glossed as "hurt", it invites a learner to write ich habe ihn zugerichtet for "I hurt him", which is badly wrong.

Bare "call" collides head-on with anrufen, the verb for telephoning, which is the reading a learner will reach for first. Zurufen is to call out to someone across a distance: er rief mir eine Warnung zu.
